blocks.text: The eagle's wings, flight, nest, sight and food.

Scripture commends the eagle's wings for their size, Ezechielis XVII, 3. A great eagle with great wings, long-winged, etc. And there the Greeks have Ὁ ἀετὸς ὁ μέγας, ὁ μεγάλου πτέρυγος, ὁ μακρὸς τῇ ἐκτάσει [Ho aetos ho megas, ho megalou pterygos, ho makros tē ektasei]. [col. 170] For the eagle both has great wings and spreads them as widely as possible in flight. Hence the poets call it τανύπτερος [tanypteros], as if one were to say with outstretched wings. Hesiod, Theogony line 523:
Καὶ οἱ ἐπ᾽ αἰετὸν ὦρσε τανύπτερον, [Kai hoi ep᾽ aieton ōrse tanypteron,]
And he roused against him an eagle with outstretched wings. And Pindar, Pyth. 5:
Τανύπτερος ἐν ὄρνιξιν αἰετὸς, [Tanypteros en ornixin aietos,]
The eagle, among birds the one with the most outstretched wings. This the greatest of poets describes thus in the last book of the Iliad, line 317:

Ὅσση δ᾽ ὑψορόφοιο θύρη θαλάμοιο τέτυκται Ἀνέρος ἀφνειοῖο εὐκληῒς ἀραρυῖα, Τόσσ᾽ ἄρα τοῦ ἑκάτερθεν ἔσαν πτερά. [Hossē d᾽ hypsorophoio thyrē thalamoio tetyktai Aneros aphneioio euklēis araryia, Toss᾽ ara tou hekaterthen esan ptera.]

As great as is the door of a rich man's lofty chamber, well bolted and skilfully wrought, so great were its wings on either side. And in Gesner, p. 206, Georg Fabricius mentions an eagle's nest found in the year 1500 between Meissen and Bresa, towns of Germany, with three chicks in it, the wings of one of which, stretched out crosswise, measured seven ells.

With these wings the eagle is borne along most swiftly and with the greatest force, especially when it swoops on its prey. Hence Apuleius, Florida book 1, says the eagle hurls itself down from above upon its prey like a thunderbolt. And in Cicero, On Divination book 2, when a runner reported to an interpreter that he had dreamed he had become an eagle, the latter said: You have won, for no bird flies more vehemently than that one. Accordingly the ancients relate that the serpent, otherwise a bold and fearless animal, is put to flight by the mere rushing sound of the eagle's wings. Aelian, Hist. book 2, ch. 26: Καὶ τόν γε τῶν πτερῶν αὐτοῦ ῥοῖζον, καὶ τὸ τῶν θηρίων ἀτρεπτότατον, ὅμως κατέπτηξεν ὁ δράκων ἀκούσας μόνον καὶ παραχρῆμα κατέδυ, καὶ ἀσμένως ἠφανίσθη [Kai ton ge tōn pterōn autou rhoizon, kai to tōn thēriōn atreptotaton, homōs kateptēxen ho drakōn akousas monon kai parachrēma katedy, kai asmenōs ēphanisthē]. Philes, ch. 1:

Τούτου δὲ καὶ τὸν ῥοῖζον ἀκούσας δράκων, Ἔπτηξέ τε παραχρῆμα, καὶ συνεστάλη, Καὶ τοὺς μυχοὺς ὑπῆλθε τοὺς ἀποκρύφους. [Toutou de kai ton rhoizon akousas drakōn, Eptēxe te parachrēma, kai synestalē, Kai tous mychous hypēlthe tous apokryphous.]

Hence Festus holds that the wind aquilo [north wind] is so called from its most vehement flight, like that of an eagle. And most think that the eagle itself is called ἀετός [aetos] in Greek from ἀΐσσειν [aïssein], [II, 751] that is, to rush with force and to swoop. We have derived it from עיט ajit, the name by which the Hebrews call a bird of prey. But it comes to much the same thing, for עיט is formed from העיט, that is, from flying at and swooping. All this serves to show that it is not without reason that Scripture so often compares the speed and force of those who rush into battle with eagles, and indeed with eagles swooping on their prey. Thus Deut. XXVIII, 49. The Lord will raise against thee a nation from afar, from the farthest ends of the earth, כאשר ידאה הנשר, as the eagle flies. The Greeks: ὡσεὶ ὅρμημα ἀετοῦ [hōsei hormēma aetou]; and Jerome: like an eagle flying with force. So in Iliad 21, line 252, Achilles, rushing upon the Trojans, is described by the Poet as αἰετοῦ οἴματ᾽ ἔχων [aietou oimat᾽ echōn], having the onrush of an eagle. For to the Scholiast οἴματα [oimata] are ὁρμήματα [hormēmata]; to Hesychius, Οἴματα· ἀετοῦ ὁρμήματα [Oimata: aetou hormēmata]. Likewise the same poet of Hector, Iliad 22, line 308:
Οἴμησεν δὲ ἀλεὶς, ὥς τ᾽ αἰετὸς ὑψιπετήεις, [Oimēsen de aleis, hōs t᾽ aietos hypsipetēeis,]

Gathering himself, he swooped with force, like a high-flying eagle. Wrongly, therefore, did Philetas want to read αἰετοῦ ὄμματ᾽ ἔχων [aietou ommat᾽ echōn], having the eyes of an eagle, instead of αἰετοῦ οἴματ᾽ ἔχων [aietou oimat᾽ echōn]. For the subject here is not the eagle's eyes but the force of its swoop. To the same point belongs David's statement that Saul and Jonathan, most warlike men, were swifter than eagles, 2 Sam. I, 23. And what Jeremiah writes of the Chaldeans, IV, 13. Their horses are swifter than eagles. And of their king, Ier. XLVIII, 40. He shall fly as an eagle, and shall spread his wings over Moab. And again Ier. XLIX, 22. He shall come up as an eagle, and fly, and spread his wings over Bozrah. And Thren. IV, 19. Our persecutors are swifter than the eagles of heaven.
